title: Chapter 62 — The Dart
paragraphs: A word concerning an incident in the last chapter.

According to the invariable custom of the fishery, the whale-boat pushes off from the ship with the headsman, or whale-killer, as temporary steersman, and the harpooner, or whale-fastener, pulling the foremost oar, the one known as the harpooner-oar. Now it takes a strong, nervy arm to strike the first iron into the fish; for often, in what is called a long dart, the heavy implement has to be flung a distance of twenty or thirty feet. But however long and exhausting the chase, the harpooner is expected to pull his oar to the utmost all the while; indeed, he is expected to set the rest an example of superhuman activity, not only by incredible rowing, but by repeated loud and fearless shouts; and what it is to keep shouting at the top of your voice while every other muscle is strained and half wrenched out of place — that no one knows but those who have tried it. For my part, I cannot bawl very heartily and work very recklessly at one and the same time. In this straining, bawling state, then, with his back to the fish, the exhausted harpooner all at once hears the exciting cry — "Stand up, and give it to him!" He now has to drop and secure his oar, turn halfway round on his center, seize his harpoon from the crotch, and with what little strength may remain, try to pitch it somehow into the whale. No wonder, taking the whole fleet of whalemen together, that out of fifty fair chances for a dart, not five are successful; no wonder that so many luckless harpooners are madly cursed and demoted; no wonder that some of them actually burst their blood-vessels in the boat; no wonder that some sperm whalemen are gone four years with four barrels; no wonder that to many shipowners whaling is nothing but a losing business; for it is the harpooner who makes the voyage, and if you take the breath out of his body, how can you expect to find it there when it is most wanted!

Then again, if the dart hits home, at the second critical moment — when the whale starts to run — the boatheader and harpooner likewise start running fore and aft, putting themselves and everyone else in imminent danger. That is when they swap places, and the headsman, the chief officer of the little craft, takes his proper post in the bow.

Now, I don't care who says otherwise: all this is both foolish and unnecessary. The headsman should stay in the bow from start to finish. He should throw both the harpoon and the lance, and no rowing at all should be expected of him, except in circumstances any fisherman would recognize. I know this would sometimes cost a little speed in the chase; but the long experience of many whalemen of more than one nation has convinced me that in the great majority of failures in the fishery, the cause has by no means been so much the whale's speed as the harpooner's exhaustion that I described earlier.
To make the dart as effective as possible, the harpooners of this world must spring to their feet from rest, not from hard labor.
